title: Export records to CSV with stable columns and every section

blocks.text: The finance team pastes the monthly CSV exports into spreadsheets that read columns by position. `CsvExport` turns a list of records into CSV, and for a sealed family of records, such as every kind of delivery, it writes one `## TypeName` section per record type, empty ones included, so every month's file has the same shape.
The writing is done. Finish the three `TODO` methods in `src/main/java/practice/CsvExport.java`:

items: `columns(...)`: the column names of a record type;
`valueOf(...)`: one record's value in one column;
`recordTypes(...)`: every record type of a sealed family, which may contain sealed interfaces of its own.

blocks.text: When you're done, a record exports exactly its own values, under columns in the order the record declares them, on any JVM, and a family export has one section per record type of the family and no others. About ten lines in total.

cases.says: each of a record's values is exported under the column of the same name
a family export has a section for every record type of a sealed interface, including types with no rows
the columns are the record's components, with no column for toString or hashCode
the header lists the columns in the order of the record header, not sorted
record types under a sealed sub-interface are part of the family
a sealed sub-interface is not itself a record type of the family

origin.section: Read a Record Through Its Components and a Sealed Type Through Its Permitted Subclasses

concepts: getPermittedSubclasses() lists only direct subtypes, in no specified order, and returns null for a type that is not sealed, so nested sealed families need a recursive walk.
getRecordComponents() returns exactly a record's components in header order, while a method scan also finds toString and hashCode.
